title: Distinct Subset Products
content: A set has distinct subset products if every pair of distinct subsets yields different products. Formally: for all S ≠ T with S, T ⊆ A, we have ∏_{a∈S} a ≠ ∏_{a∈T} a. The empty subset gives product 1 (via Finset.prod id on ∅), so no other subset can have product 1, ruling out the element 1.
mathContext: $A$ has distinct subset products if the map $S \mapsto \prod_{a \in S} a$ is injective on $\mathcal{P}(A)$. Since $|\mathcal{P}(A)| = 2^{|A|}$, the products must span at least $2^{|A|}$ distinct values in $\{1, \ldots, n^{|A|}\}$.

title: The Function g(n)
content: g(n) is the maximum cardinality of a subset of {1,...,n} with distinct subset products. Defined using Finset.sup over the powerset of {0,...,n} filtered by the distinct products property. This is noncomputable because the filter predicate involves quantification over all pairs of subsets.
mathContext: $g(n) = \max\{|A| : A \subseteq \{1, \ldots, n\}, \text{ all subset products distinct}\}$. The prime number theorem gives $g(n) \sim \pi(n) \sim n/\log n$.

title: Prime Counting Function π(n)
content: Defines primePi(n) = π(n) as the count of primes ≤ n, implemented by filtering Finset.range(n+1) with Nat.Prime. The prime number theorem gives π(n) ~ n/log n, which is the dominant term in g(n).
mathContext: $\pi(n) = |\{p \leq n : p \text{ prime}\}|$. By PNT, $\pi(n) = \frac{n}{\log n}(1 + o(1))$. The second-order term $\pi(\sqrt{n}) \sim 2\sqrt{n}/\log n$ is the key correction for $g(n)$.

title: Erdős's Upper Bound (1966)
content: Erdős (1966) proved g(n) ≤ π(n) + O(n^{1/2}/log n). The idea: elements of A beyond the primes must be composite, and each composite number 'uses up' prime factors that could conflict with other composites. The error term O(n^{1/2}/log n) ≈ O(π(√n)) comes from counting how many composites can coexist.
mathContext: $g(n) \leq \pi(n) + C \cdot \frac{n^{1/2}}{\log n}$ for some absolute constant $C > 0$ and all $n \geq 2$.

title: Erdős's Conjecture (Main Question)
content: Erdős asked whether g(n) ≤ π(n) + π(√n) + o(n^{1/2}/log n). This would show the construction using primes plus prime squares is essentially optimal. The formalization uses the ε-N definition of little-o: for every ε > 0, the inequality holds for all sufficiently large n.
mathContext: $g(n) \leq \pi(n) + \pi(\sqrt{n}) + o\left(\frac{n^{1/2}}{\log n}\right)$, where $o(f)$ means: for every $\varepsilon > 0$, $|\text{error}| \leq \varepsilon \cdot f(n)$ for large $n$.

title: Raghavan's Upper Bound (2025)
content: Raghavan (2025) proved g(n) ≤ π(n) + π(√n) + O(n^{5/12+o(1)}). The error term n^{5/12} ≈ n^{0.417} is much smaller than the conjectured o(n^{1/2}/log n) ≈ o(n^{0.5}/log n), giving a stronger result than Erdős asked for. The exponent 5/12 comes from exponential sum estimates in the proof.
mathContext: $g(n) \leq \pi(n) + \pi(\sqrt{n}) + O(n^{5/12+o(1)})$. Since $5/12 < 1/2$, this implies $n^{5/12} = o(n^{1/2}/\log n)$, confirming Erdős's conjecture.

title: Raghavan's Lower Bound
content: Raghavan also proved g(n) ≥ π(n) + π(√n) + π(∛n)/3 - O(1). The lower bound construction uses: all primes ≤ n (contributing π(n)), squares p² of primes p ≤ √n (contributing π(√n)), and about π(∛n)/3 cubes p³ of primes p ≤ ∛n. The cube contributions are possible because p³ adds exponent 3 to p, distinguishable from 0, 1, or 2.
mathContext: $g(n) \geq \pi(n) + \pi(\sqrt{n}) + \frac{\pi(n^{1/3})}{3} - O(1)$. Combined with the upper bound, this gives $g(n) = \pi(n) + \pi(\sqrt{n}) + \Theta(\pi(n^{1/3}))$.

title: Conjecture Confirmed
content: The main theorem: Erdős's conjecture is TRUE. For large n, Raghavan's upper bound implies the conjectured bound since n^{5/12} = o(n^{1/2}/log n). The proof uses intro and sorry for the asymptotic argument bridging the two error terms.
mathContext: Since $n^{5/12+o(1)} = o(n^{1/2}/\log n)$ (because $5/12 < 1/2$), Raghavan's bound confirms $g(n) \leq \pi(n) + \pi(\sqrt{n}) + o(n^{1/2}/\log n)$.

title: Primes Have Distinct Products
content: The set of primes ≤ n automatically has distinct subset products by the fundamental theorem of arithmetic. Different subsets of primes yield products with different prime factorizations, hence different values. This gives the baseline g(n) ≥ π(n).
mathContext: If $A \subseteq \{p : p \leq n, p \text{ prime}\}$, then $S \neq T \subseteq A$ implies $\prod_{s \in S} s \neq \prod_{t \in T} t$ by unique factorization in $\mathbb{Z}$.

title: Adding Prime Squares Preserves Property
content: Adding squares of small primes (p² for p ≤ √n) to the set of primes maintains distinct products. Including p² allows the exponent of p in any subset product to be 0, 1, 2, or 3 (from none, p only, p² only, or both), and these four values are distinguishable.
mathContext: For $P = \{p \leq n : p \text{ prime}\}$ and $P^2 = \{p^2 : p \leq \sqrt{n}, p \text{ prime}\}$, $P \cup P^2$ has distinct subset products. The exponent of prime $p$ in $\prod_{a \in S} a$ encodes membership of $p$ and $p^2$ in $S$.

title: Structure of Optimal Sets
content: Raghavan's structural result: any optimal set A (achieving g(n)) decomposes as P ∪ P² ∪ R, where P consists of primes, P² consists of prime squares, and the remainder R has |R| ≤ π(∛n)/2. This shows optimal sets are 'almost' the natural construction, with only a small correction from higher prime powers.
mathContext: If $|A| = g(n)$ and $A$ has distinct subset products, then $A = P \cup P^2 \cup R$ with $P \subseteq \text{primes}$, $P^2 \subseteq \{p^2\}$, and $|R| \leq \pi(n^{1/3})/2$.

title: Error Term Comparison (Aristotle-Proved)
content: Aristotle proved that n^{5/12} ≤ C · n^{1/2}/log n for some C > 0 and n ≥ 4. This bridges Raghavan's error term to Erdős's, confirming the conjecture. The proof uses suffices to reduce to a multiplicative form, then applies positivity and nlinarith after algebraic manipulation via div_mul_cancel₀.
mathContext: $n^{5/12} \leq C \cdot \frac{n^{1/2}}{\log n}$ iff $n^{5/12} \cdot \log n \leq C \cdot n^{1/2}$, i.e., $\log n \leq C \cdot n^{1/12}$. This holds since $\log n = o(n^\varepsilon)$ for any $\varepsilon > 0$.

title: Multiplicative Sidon Set
content: A multiplicative Sidon set satisfies: if a·b = c·d with a, b, c, d ∈ A, then {a,b} = {c,d} as multisets. This is a stronger condition than distinct subset products—it forbids even pairwise product collisions. The definition in the file is split across lines due to Aristotle parsing issues.
mathContext: $A$ is multiplicative Sidon if $ab = cd$ with $a, b, c, d \in A$ implies $\{a, b\} = \{c, d\}$. Classical (additive) Sidon sets satisfy $a + b = c + d \Rightarrow \{a,b\} = \{c,d\}$ and have size $O(\sqrt{n})$.

title: Sidon Implies Distinct Products
content: Every multiplicative Sidon set has distinct subset products, since Sidon is a stronger condition. But the converse fails: distinct products is a strictly weaker condition, as demonstrated by explicit counterexamples.
mathContext: Sidon $\Rightarrow$ distinct products: if $\prod_{s \in S} s = \prod_{t \in T} t$ with $S \neq T$, we can find $a, b, c, d$ with $ab = cd$ and $\{a,b\} \neq \{c,d\}$, contradicting Sidon.

title: Example: {2, 3, 5} Has Distinct Products
content: The set {2, 3, 5} has 2³ = 8 subsets with products: ∅→1, {2}→2, {3}→3, {5}→5, {2,3}→6, {2,5}→10, {3,5}→15, {2,3,5}→30. All 8 values are distinct, illustrating the primes-only construction for g(5) ≥ 3.
mathContext: The 8 subset products of $\{2, 3, 5\}$ are $\{1, 2, 3, 5, 6, 10, 15, 30\}$—all distinct by unique factorization of primes.

title: Counterexample: {2, 3, 6} Fails
content: The set {2, 3, 6} does NOT have distinct products: the subset {6} has product 6, and the subset {2, 3} also has product 2·3 = 6. Including composite numbers that are products of existing elements always creates such collisions.
mathContext: $\{6\}$ gives product 6, and $\{2, 3\}$ gives $2 \cdot 3 = 6$. The collision $6 = 2 \cdot 3$ violates injectivity of the product map on $\mathcal{P}(\{2,3,6\})$.
